plan: Harder SAT items: literary inference, a selection-effect alternative explanation, neither/nor agreement, a three-part synthesis goal, a qualified-agreement view, and a 'less ___' negation word item.

passages.title: The letter
passages.text:
The following text is from a short story. Mrs. Hale has just received a letter.
She read the letter twice, the second time more slowly, as though the words might rearrange themselves into something kinder if given the opportunity. They did not. She folded it along its creases, laid it upon the mantel beside the clock, and turned to the window, where the afternoon was going about its business with a composure she could not help resenting.

passages.title: EV survey
passages.text: A survey asked drivers to name their greatest concern about electric vehicles. Among current owners of electric vehicles, 35% named the availability of charging stations; among drivers who had considered buying one but decided against it, 70% did. One might conclude that owning an electric vehicle eases worries about charging. But because the second group consists entirely of people who chose not to buy, the difference may instead reflect the fact that ______

passages.title: Foundation soil
passages.text: Neither the architect nor the engineers ______ aware that the soil beneath the building site had been filled in decades earlier, a fact that came to light only when cracks appeared in the new foundation.

passages.title: Transit hours
passages.text: The decision by the city's transit authority to extend service hours on weekends and holidays ______ riders who work late shifts, many of whom previously had to pay for taxis to get home.

passages.title: Drought varieties
passages.text: Researchers expected that a drought-resistant wheat variety would outperform the standard variety most clearly in the driest years. ______ in the driest year of the five-year study, the two varieties produced nearly identical yields; the drought-resistant variety's advantage appeared only in years of moderate dryness.

passages.title: Proof notes
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In 2022, mathematician Leah Okonjo proved the Harbor Conjecture.
• The conjecture concerns how many ways a network of points can be connected without forming loops.
• It had remained unsolved for 70 years.
• Okonjo's proof uses a technique from probability theory.
• Other mathematicians have since used her technique on related problems.

passages.title: Printing press
passages.text: Many historians have argued that the printing press spread quickly across Europe because it dramatically lowered the cost of books. Historian Imre Halasz agrees that printing eventually made books cheaper, but he notes that in the first decades after its introduction, printed books often sold for about as much as manuscripts did. He also observes that the earliest presses clustered in cities that already had universities and established book trades.

passages.title: Novelist themes
passages.text: The novelist's later work is far less ______ than her early fiction: where the early books announce their themes in the first chapter, the later ones withhold them until the final pages, if they disclose them at all.

passages.title: Expedition water
passages.text: The expedition's success depended on a single resource ______ fresh water, which had to be carried in from a spring two days' walk away.

passages.title: Recycling rates
passages.text:
City A began offering curbside composting in 2016; City B did not.
Year | City A recycling rate | City B recycling rate
2015 | 22% | 30%
2018 | 31% | 32%
2021 | 38% | 33%
Although City B had the higher recycling rate in 2015, ______

candidates.stem: Based on the text, Mrs. Hale's reaction to the letter is best described as

choices.A: relief that the news is not as bad as she had feared.
choices.B: confusion about what the writer of the letter meant.
choices.C: disappointment that she tries to keep under control.
choices.D: indifference toward news that she had long expected.

candidates.evidence: as though the words might rearrange themselves into something kinder
candidates.explanation: She hopes the words will become "kinder" (the news is bad), but she folds the letter neatly and sets it aside (restraint) while resenting the calm afternoon (suppressed feeling).

A.rationale: She hopes the words will become "kinder," and they do not, so the news is unwelcome.

B.rationale: She rereads it hoping it will change, not because she cannot understand it.

D.rationale: Resenting the afternoon's composure shows she is not indifferent.

hints: What does she hope the words will do?
What do her careful actions suggest about how she handles her feelings?

strategy.explanation: Combine the hope for kinder words with her controlled actions.

candidates.remember: Characters often show feelings through actions, not statements.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: drivers most worried about charging were the least likely to buy an electric vehicle in the first place.
choices.B: owners discover after buying that charging stations are more common than they had expected.
choices.C: electric vehicles have become noticeably less expensive to purchase in recent years.
choices.D: most drivers do not consider charging availability at all when choosing which car to buy.

candidates.evidence: because the second group consists entirely of people who chose not to buy
candidates.explanation: The "But" sentence offers an alternative to "ownership eases worry": the groups were sorted by their decision, so people who worried most about charging may simply have chosen not to buy.

B.rationale: This restates the conclusion the text is questioning (that ownership eases worry).

C.rationale: Price does not explain why the two groups differ in concern about charging.

D.rationale: The survey shows many drivers do name charging as their top concern.

hints: What conclusion does the "But" sentence push back on?
How were the two groups formed?

strategy.explanation: The blank must offer an explanation different from the one already stated.

candidates.remember: An alternative explanation must differ from the claim being questioned.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: Neither the architect nor the engineers
candidates.explanation: In a "neither ... nor" subject, the verb agrees with the subject closer to it. "Engineers" is plural and the events are past, so "were."

A.rationale: With "neither ... nor," the verb agrees with the nearer subject, "engineers," which is plural.

C.rationale: "Has" is singular, but the nearer subject "engineers" is plural.

D.rationale: "Is" is singular and present tense, but the nearer subject is plural and the narration is past.

hints: Which subject is closer to the verb?

strategy.explanation: Apply the nearer-subject rule, then check tense.

candidates.remember: With neither/nor, match the verb to the nearer subject.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.evidence: The decision by the city's transit authority
candidates.explanation: The subject is "decision," which is singular; the phrases that follow modify it. No punctuation belongs between subject and verb.

C.rationale: A comma should not separate a subject from its verb.

D.rationale: A dash should not separate the subject from its verb, and "have" is plural.

hints: Strip the prepositional phrases: what is the subject?

strategy.explanation: Remove punctuation choices first, then check agreement.

candidates.remember: Don't separate a subject from its verb with punctuation.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: Researchers expected that a drought-resistant wheat variety would outperform
candidates.explanation: The researchers expected the biggest advantage in the driest years, but the varieties performed alike then. "Yet" signals the contrast with the expectation.

A.rationale: "Indeed" would confirm the expectation, but the result contradicts it.

B.rationale: The result was not what researchers expected.

D.rationale: "Moreover" adds a similar point, but the result contrasts with the expectation.

hints: Did the result match the expectation?
candidates.remember: An "expected" sentence often sets up a contrast.

candidates.subskill: Rhetorical synthesis (significance for a new audience)
candidates.stem: The student wants to emphasize the significance of Okonjo's proof to an audience unfamiliar with the Harbor Conjecture. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: In 2022, Leah Okonjo proved the Harbor Conjecture by applying a technique drawn from probability theory.
choices.B: Okonjo's 2022 proof settled a 70-year-old question about linking points without loops, and others now use her method.
choices.C: The Harbor Conjecture, unsolved for 70 years, concerns how points in a network can be linked without loops.
choices.D: Leah Okonjo's proof of the Harbor Conjecture relies on probability, which others have since applied too.

candidates.evidence: It had remained unsolved for 70 years.
candidates.explanation: An unfamiliar audience needs the problem explained, and significance needs evidence: the 70-year wait and the method's later use. B gives all three.

A.rationale: This names the conjecture without explaining it and gives no sign of significance.

C.rationale: This explains the conjecture but never mentions Okonjo's proof.

D.rationale: This suggests influence but does not explain the conjecture for an unfamiliar audience.

hints: What does an unfamiliar audience need?

strategy.explanation: Turn the goal into a checklist: explain, credit Okonjo, show significance.

candidates.remember: Audience and purpose both shape the best choice.

candidates.stem: Based on the text, which choice best describes Halasz's view of the explanation offered by many historians?

choices.A: He rejects it entirely, arguing that printed books never became cheaper than handwritten manuscripts.
choices.B: He accepts it fully and adds evidence that early printed books cost far less than manuscripts.
choices.C: He considers it irrelevant, because universities and booksellers rarely purchased printed books.
choices.D: He considers it incomplete, since the press's early spread seems tied more to existing demand than to lower prices.

candidates.evidence: printed books often sold for about as much as manuscripts did
candidates.explanation: Halasz grants that books eventually got cheaper but points out that early on prices were similar, and presses went where demand already existed. So he sees the cost explanation as incomplete for the early spread.

A.rationale: Halasz "agrees that printing eventually made books cheaper."

B.rationale: He says early printed books cost about as much as manuscripts.

C.rationale: The text never says universities avoided printed books; it says presses clustered near them.

hints: What two observations complicate the cost explanation?

strategy.explanation: Eliminate choices that ignore his partial agreement.

candidates.remember: "Agrees ... but" signals a qualified, not total, rejection.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: the later ones withhold them until the final pages
candidates.explanation: The later books hide their themes, so they are less "overt" (open, obvious) than the early books, which announce theirs at once.

B.rationale: The colon contrasts how openly themes are revealed, not the scope of the books.

D.rationale: "Less subtle" would mean more obvious, the opposite of withholding themes.

hints: Do the later books reveal their themes more or less openly?
Watch the word "less" before the blank.

strategy.explanation: Predict "open" for the blank, keeping "less" in mind.

candidates.remember: Account for negating words like "less" before the blank.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.explanation: A colon after a complete clause introduces what "a single resource" refers to: fresh water.

A.rationale: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but "fresh water ..." is not one.

B.rationale: "That" turns the rest into a broken clause with no verb for "fresh water."

C.rationale: "And" wrongly presents fresh water as a second item rather than the resource itself.

strategy.explanation: Test what each mark requires on its right side.

candidates.remember: Use a colon to introduce an item that explains what came before.

candidates.stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to complete the statement?

choices.A: City B's recycling rate rose in each year shown in the table, from 30% to 33%.
choices.B: City A's rate surpassed City B's by 2021, after rising 16 points to City B's 3.
choices.C: City A's recycling rate was still slightly lower than City B's rate in 2018.
choices.D: both cities had recycling rates above 30% in 2018, though City B's was higher.

candidates.evidence: Although City B had the higher recycling rate in 2015
candidates.explanation: "Although" calls for a contrast with City B's 2015 lead. By 2021 City A led, 38% to 33%, after gaining 16 points to City B's 3.

A.rationale: This is true but does not contrast with City B's early lead.

C.rationale: This continues City B's lead rather than contrasting with it.

D.rationale: This does not show the reversal that "Although" sets up.

hints: What does "Although" require the second half to do?

strategy.explanation: Use the sentence's structure to predict a reversal.

candidates.remember: "Although" sets up a contrast; the completion must deliver it.
